info.name: Blendy · User Journeys
info.description:
Ordered workflows that chain into each other — run a folder top to bottom in the Collection Runner and it executes unattended.

**Run J1 first.** It creates the shop, catalogue and stock that every later journey uses, and captures the ids into collection variables.

**Setup**
1. `python manage.py migrate` — seeds the RBAC catalogue
2. `python manage.py createsuperuser`
3. Start the server with the webhook token set:
   `MPESA_WEBHOOK_TOKEN=tok-123 MPESA_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE_IP=false python manage.py runserver`
4. Set `superadmin_email` and `superadmin_password` below

Every request asserts its own outcome, so a red run tells you which step broke rather than leaving you to compare payloads.

variable.description: From manage.py createsuperuser. Needed to onboard a shop.
Must equal MPESA_WEBHOOK_TOKEN on the server.
Kept so J6 can switch back.
Captured in J1. Sent as X-Organization.
The sellable unit every journey trades in.
Echoed back on the STK callback.
Captured by J9 step 2 from GET /api/organization/platform/. HQ is not listed by GET /api/organization/, which returns customers only.

item.name: J1 · Open a shop
item.description:
Everything a new shop needs before it can sell anything: an organization, an owner, a priced catalogue, and stock on the shelf.

**Run this first.** Every later journey uses the organization, variation and token it captures.

request.description: Only a superadmin may onboard an organization.

Creates the organization, its Default Pricelist, its ORG_ADMIN owner, and enables the built-in roles — one transaction.

The returned organization id is what every later request sends as X-Organization.
Onboarding created it. Without a pricelist the shop cannot price or sell anything, so this is worth checking before going further.

item.name: 6. Create a product with priced variations

request.description:
At least one variation is required and each must carry a selling_price.

`cost_price` stays on the variation; `selling_price` is written to the Default Pricelist. You write `selling_price` and read back `price`.

exec: pm.test('price came back from the pricelist', () =>

request.description: Writes a STOCK_IN entry to the ledger and updates the cached balance in the same transaction. `available_quantity` in the response is recomputed from the ledger, so it doubles as a check that the two agree.

item.name: J2 · Sell, and get paid by STK push
item.description:
The daily loop, happy path. The customer's phone prompts, they enter their PIN, Safaricom calls back, the sale is PAID.

Step 3 stands in for Safaricom. Point `base_url` at a local server started with `MPESA_WEBHOOK_TOKEN=tok-123 MPESA_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE_IP=false`.

request.description:
`unit_price` is optional — omit it and the pricelist price applies. Supply it and it must match exactly.

Creating the sale decrements stock through the ledger in the same transaction.

`amount` must equal the sale total. The phone number is normalised to +254 and checked against Safaricom prefixes.

The result arrives on the webhook, not in this response — the payment comes back PENDING.

**Safaricom calls this, not your client.** The token in the URL is the shared secret, since Safaricom does not sign callbacks.

Change `Amount` to 300.00 and re-run: the sale stays UNPAID and the payment is flagged MISMATCH. A success callback for the wrong amount never marks a sale paid.

item.name: J3 · STK push fails, customer pays the Till
item.description:
MVP §8 / US-9b / US-9c — the fallback that matters most in a real shop.

The push fails, but the sale is **not** closed. It moves to AWAITING_DIRECT_PAYMENT, the customer pays the Till from the M-Pesa menu, and the incoming C2B confirmation is matched back to the sale by phone number and amount.

request.description: Any non-zero ResultCode. 1032 is a user cancel.

item.name: 4. The sale is queued, not closed

request.description: The owner's queue for anything still owed — sales awaiting a direct payment, and sales never paid at all.

exec: pm.test('our sale is awaiting a direct payment', () =>

request.description:
A direct payment has no CheckoutRequestID, so it is attributed to a tenant by BusinessShortCode and matched to an open sale by MSISDN + TransAmount inside a 24-hour window.

Matching is idempotent on TransID — re-run this and nothing double-counts.

item.name: 6. The sale is reconciled to PAID
J4 · A direct payment that matches nothing
item.description: US-10. Money arrives that cannot be tied to an open sale — no candidate, or more than one. It is **not** dropped and **not** guessed at: it waits in a queue with a note saying why.

request.description: Still answers 200 in Safaricom's expected shape, so it stops retrying — but `matched` is false.

item.name: J5 · Stock runs low and is replenished
item.description: US-3, US-17, US-19. Stock is a ledger, not a number: every change is an entry, and the balance is a cache of those entries.

request.description: Leaves the variation at or below its reorder_level of 10.

item.name: 2. The low-stock queue picks it up

request.description: The threshold is **inclusive** — selling down *to* it fires the alert, not only going under. Most urgent first.

Send **exactly one** of `counted_quantity` (the figure on the shelf) or `quantity` (a signed change).

`reason` is never optional — an unexplained adjustment is what the ledger exists to rule out.

The difference is computed under the row lock that writes it, so a sale landing mid-count cannot be silently undone.
Append-only and read-only. A POST here returns 405 — stock moves through the restock, adjust and sale paths only, so the balance can never drift from the entries that explain it.

exec: pm.test('shows stock in, sale and adjustment', () => {

item.name: 6. The ledger cannot be written directly
J6 · Hire a cashier
item.description: US-15. A cashier records sales and sees stock, but cannot change prices, move stock, or manage staff.

item.name: 1. See which roles the shop has enabled

request.description: Onboarding enables ORG_ADMIN, CASHIER and VIEWER. To enable another, POST {"role_id": "..."} here — the organization comes from the header, never the body.
The sharpest owner/till line: a cashier sells stock down but cannot restock or adjust it, so the ledger's write path stays with whoever is accountable for the count.

item.name: 8. Log back in as the owner

request.description: Restores the owner token for the remaining journeys.

item.name: J7 · Guest checkout
item.description: A walk-in customer with no account. Two endpoints stay open to anonymous callers — creating a sale and paying for it — and nothing else does.

request.description: Deliberately not permission-gated on any role: a customer at the till holds no role at all.
Rate limited when anonymous — 5/hour per phone number, 20/hour per IP — because it fires an STK push at a caller-supplied number. Run it six times to see a 429.

item.name: J8 · Guardrails
item.description: The refusals worth knowing before you build a UI, since each one is an error state a form has to handle.

item.name: 1. A price that does not match the pricelist

request.description: Prices are never taken on trust. Any concession must be declared in `discount`, where it stays visible, rather than hidden in a reduced unit price.

item.name: 3. A product whose variation has no price

request.description: A product with no priced variation is not sellable, so it is refused rather than created.

item.name: 4. A product with no variations at all
5. An anonymous caller granting themselves a discount

request.description: Guest checkout stays open, but it cannot discount itself.
On a write this is a 403. On a **read** the queryset resolves to no tenant and returns an empty page rather than an error — the viewsets fail closed, so a forgotten header looks like an empty shop.

item.name: 7. A webhook with the wrong token
J9 · HQ: support a shop without the superadmin flag
item.description:
Blendy's own staff. HQ is an organization like any other as far as RBAC is concerned, which is what lets platform staff use the same roles a shop's staff use.

**Setup.** `python manage.py bootstrap_hq` prints the HQ id — put it in `hq_organization_id`. HQ is deliberately absent from `GET /api/organization/`, which lists customers only.

Run **J1** first; this journey supports the shop J1 created.

request.description: The flag is retained as break-glass. Everything after this step uses roles instead.

HQ is deliberately absent from `GET /api/organization/`, which lists customers only — so this is how platform staff learn the id they send as X-Organization when working on HQ itself. Open to any holder of a `platform.*` permission.

exec: pm.test('it really is the platform org', () =>

request.description: PLATFORM_ADMIN and SUPPORT_AGENT are enabled on HQ only — never on a shop.

item.name: 6. Log in as the platform admin
7. Onboard a shop — no flag involved

request.description: This used to require `is_superuser_admin`. It now needs `platform.onboard_organization`, which is grantable and revocable per person.

item.name: 8. Read the shop's sales to help them

request.description: Crossing the tenant boundary. The shop's own staff are unaffected; this request is what the access log exists to record.

exec: pm.test('support can see the shop', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: 9. Log in as the support agent

request.description: `platform.access_tenants` is a read grant. Writing needs `platform.act_as_tenant`, which SUPPORT_AGENT does not hold — and it holds no tenant write permission either, so both layers refuse independently.

item.name: 12. Support cannot read the access log

request.description: Reading who watched whom is an administrator's business.

item.name: 13. Log back in as the platform admin
14. Every crossing is on the record

request.description: Grants *and* denials, including the support agent's refused write above. Read-only for everyone — POST, PATCH and DELETE all return 405, superadmin included.

item.name: 15. The shop can see it too

request.description:
The tenant-facing half. The same records, shown to the organization they are about — an assurance worth little if it depended on us answering.

Run this as the shop owner from J1 to see the real thing: Blendy staff are named, while a *different* customer whose access was refused appears without being identified. Naming them would hand one shop another shop's staff email.

exec: pm.test('platform admin can read it as the tenant', () =>
